{{Short description|Former statistical region of Wales}}
[[File:NUTS 3 regions of Wales map.svg|thumb|The region consisted of the green [[principal areas of Wales]] on this map, with [[East Wales]] in shades of brown.]]
'''West Wales and the Valleys''' was a UK [[International Territorial Level]] 2 [[Regions of Wales#Statistical regions|statistical region]] covering the western areas of [[Wales]] and the [[South Wales Valleys]]. Created as part of [[Eurostat]]'s [[Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics]] (NUTS), it was used by the [[European Union]] (EU) to deliver the [[European Regional Development Fund]] to areas of Wales, until [[Brexit|the UK's withdrawal from the EU]] in 2020, after which it was mirrored onto the [[Office for National Statistics]]' International Territorial Level (ITL) geo-classification system. The remainder of Wales was part of the [[East Wales]] statistical region. It was replaced in 2025, by three alternative regions of Wales.<ref>{{Cite web |title=International geographies - Office for National Statistics |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/geography/ukgeographies/eurostat#wales |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=www.ons.gov.uk}}</ref>

==Description==
The statistical region covered all of western Wales from [[Denbighshire]] in the north, to the [[South Wales Valleys]] and covering [[Bridgend County Borough|Bridgend]], [[Swansea]], [[Neath Port Talbot]], as well as the [[Isle of Anglesey]] off the north-west coast of Wales.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=What Europe does for me - #EUandME |url=https://what-europe-does-for-me.eu/en/portal/1/UKL1 |access-date=2024-01-06 |website=what-europe-does-for-me.eu |language=en}}</ref> It covers an area of {{Convert|1240000|ha|km2}}, with a coastline of {{Convert|1150|km|mi}}. In September 2010, it had around 1.28 million  people, 64% of the [[Demographics of Wales|population of Wales]], although 60% of the statistical region's population resided in the South Wales Valleys.<ref>{{Cite web |title=West Wales and the Valleys Convergence Operational Programme European Regional Development Fund 2007-2013 |url=https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/publications/2019-09/west-wales-and-the-valleys-european-regional-development-fund-operational-programme-2007-to-2013.pdf |website=gov.wales |publisher=Welsh European Funding Office}}</ref> The region was greatly impacted by the loss of its [[Mining in Wales|mining]] and heavy industry.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Smit |first=Josephine |date=2016-09-20 |title=What did the EU do for Wales? |url=https://www.ribaj.com/intelligence/what-did-the-eu-do-for-wales |access-date=2024-01-07 |website=www.ribaj.com |language=en}}</ref>

The 15 [[principal areas of Wales]]<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |date=2016-06-09 |title=What next for Wales' European funding? |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-politics-eu-referendum-36417964 |access-date=2024-01-07 |work=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref> that were part of the region are: [[Blaenau Gwent]], [[Bridgend County Borough|Bridgend]], [[Caerphilly County Borough|Caerphilly]], [[Carmarthenshire]], [[Ceredigion]], [[Conwy County Borough|Conwy]], [[Denbighshire]], [[Gwynedd]], [[Isle of Anglesey]], [[Merthyr Tydfil County Borough|Merthyr Tydfil]], [[Neath Port Talbot]], [[Pembrokeshire]], [[Rhondda Cynon Taf]], [[Swansea]] and [[Torfaen]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 2014 |title=European Structural Fund Programme Regions in Wales for 2014-2020 |url=https://www.cardiff.ac.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0009/519273/Structural-Fund-regions-in-Wales-map.pdf |website=[[Cardiff University|cardiff.ac.uk]] |publisher=[[Welsh Government]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2012-03-14 |title=Valleys, north and west Wales economic figures 'misleading', claims government |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-wales-17363491 |access-date=2024-01-07 |work=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref>

The region was used to manage [[European Regional Development Fund|European Union (EU) funding]] to this part of the [[United Kingdom]],<ref name=":0" /> with the funding applied in seven-year periods.<ref name=":2" /> Between 2014 and 2020, €1.2 billion was allocated to the regions classified as 'less developed'<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 2019 |title=West Wales and the Valleys European Regional Development Fund Programme 2014-2020 - 2017 Annual Implementation Report - Summary |url=https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/publications/2019-08/west-wales-and-the-valleys-erdf-annual-implementation-report-2017-summary.pdf |website=gov.wales |publisher=[[Welsh Government]]}}</ref> by the EU,  having a [[GDP per capita of British regions|GDP per capita]] lower than 75% of the EU average.<ref name=":1" /> In 2016, the region had been awarded the highest level of structural (convergence) funding in the UK for a third time, compared to the two occasions on which [[Cornwall]], [[Liverpool]] and [[Scotland]]'s [[Highlands and Islands]] have received the highest level too. The funding is aimed at countries which have a [[gross value added]] (GVA) that is less than three quarters of the EU average. The region was awarded the highest level again, because while the region's GVA has increased, it had not increased as much as the EU average did.<ref name=":2" /> The region was also specifically awarded "special financial assistance" by the EU,<ref name=":3">{{Cite news |last=Elliott |first=Larry |date=2023-06-03 |title='We're crap at capitalism. We need something different': the battle for economic revival in the Welsh valleys |url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2023/jun/03/were-crap-at-capitalism-we-need-something-different-the-battle-for-economic-revival-in-the-welsh-valleys |access-date=2024-01-07 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0029-7712}}</ref> alongside [[South West England]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brien |first=Philip |date=11 September 2020 |title=EU funding in the UK |url=https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-7847/ |website=commonslibrary.parliament.uk |publisher=[[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] Library}}</ref>

Following the UK's withdrawal from the European Union ([[Brexit]]), disputes over continued funding for the region were raised. The [[Welsh Government]] argued that it is not receiving the same levels of funding from the UK Government as the EU had provided, while the UK Government states it is fully replacing the EU funds for the regions. The UK Government, however, awards the funds under a more competitive bidding system, compared to the EU which set overall objectives but let priorities be decided locally.<ref name=":3" /> Also, as a result of Brexit, [[Eurostat]]'s [[Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics]] (NUTS), was replaced by the UK [[Office for National Statistics]]' [[International Territorial Level]] (ITL), a similar geoclassification system that is currently a mirror of the pre-existing NUTS regions.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=International geographies - Office for National Statistics |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/geography/ukgeographies/eurostat |access-date=2024-01-07 |website=www.ons.gov.uk}}</ref>

West Wales and the Valleys was an ITL 2 area, comprising eight ITL 3 areas, which were either individuals or groupings of the principal areas of Wales. The ITL 3 areas were:<ref name=":4" />

* [[Bridgend County Borough|Bridgend]] and [[Neath Port Talbot]] (17)
* [[Conwy County Borough|Conwy]] and [[Denbighshire]] (13)
* Central [[South Wales Valleys|Valleys]] (15)
* Gwent [[South Wales Valleys|Valleys]] (16)
* [[Gwynedd]] (12)
* [[Isle of Anglesey]] (11)
* South West Wales (corresponding to former [[Dyfed]]) (14)
* [[Swansea]] (18)

''The numbers in parentheses afterwards reference those used on the map at the top of this article.''
